correctness.rationale: A finite exhaustive proof is encoded in a standard C++17 program whose bound is exactly 2339. It enumerates all 345 odd primes and all 369924 nonzero candidate indices using inverse-factorial and direct-Horner independent formulas, agreeing at every prime and producing the complete 345-row root census. The six Q/p residues are 843,1662,1732,24,685,1079, all nonzero mod 2339. Direct modular evaluation verifies six distinct second-level lifts. Miska 2014 Theorem 1 then supplies unique lifting for every exponent; all classes are accounted for because each projects to a first-level root.

originality.rationale: The original 2013 work and Miska 2014 give the object, partial census and conditional lifting theorem; Miska explicitly poses the multiplicity-existence problem. The 2017 generalization gives a six-root example only for a different polynomial h. No identified primary result or exact database establishes the least six-root prime 2339 and its six ordinary Schenker branches. value.rationale: Miska 2014 Question 4 asks whether any prime supports m Schenker zeros for each m, and the published table exhibits at most five for its first 200 primes. The new result resolves the first outstanding threshold m=6, identifies the sharp first-prime cutoff, enumerates all six residues, and proves six disjoint nonzero p-adic zero branches at every depth. This is a natural exact invariant and certificate-based finite classification motivated by a published open existence question, not an arbitrary unmotivated modulus slice. It does not claim to resolve m>=7.
